howItWorks.title: How Thought Labeling Works
howItWorks.description1: When you are anxious, thoughts can feel overwhelming and completely true. Labeling them helps you step back: a thought is a passing mental event, not necessarily reality. Naming what is happening ('worry', 'doubt', 'catastrophe') creates a small space between you and the thought.
howItWorks.description2: Moving from 'I am anxious' to 'I am having an anxious thought' changes your relationship with that thought. Instead of being carried away, you observe it. This approach is used in several therapies, including Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and mindfulness.
howItWorks.description3: With practice, you recognise your usual thoughts more quickly: 'There's my catastrophe thought again.' Recognising them lets you choose how to respond rather than react automatically.

cognitiveDefusion.title: Stepping back
cognitiveDefusion.description: Naming a thought helps you detach from it and take it less at face value.

emotionalRegulation.title: Easing emotion
emotionalRegulation.description: Putting words to what you feel often makes the emotion less intense.

patternRecognition.title: Spotting habits
patternRecognition.description: Regular labeling reveals recurring thoughts and makes them easier to recognise.

science.title: What Studies Say
science.description: Thought labeling comes from mindfulness and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. It has not been tested on its own, but programmes that use it have been well studied.
science.bottomLine: naming your thoughts and emotions helps you step back. This skill can be learned and grows stronger with practice, ideally within a programme or with professional support.

mbsr.title: A mindfulness programme compared with a medication
mbsr.type: Large trial with a comparison group
mbsr.who: 276 adults with an anxiety disorder (generalized anxiety, social anxiety, panic disorder, agoraphobia), in the United States.
mbsr.what: An 8-week mindfulness programme (weekly classes and daily practice), compared with an antidepressant (escitalopram).
mbsr.result: After 8 weeks, the mindfulness programme worked as well as the medication in reducing anxiety.
mbsr.caution: The programme requires real commitment (2.5-hour classes and 45 minutes of daily practice); it does not replace medical advice about treatment.

naming.title: Putting feelings into words
naming.what: During a brain scan, naming the emotion on a face ('anger', 'fear') rather than just looking at it.
naming.result: Naming the emotion reduced activity in the amygdala, a brain area involved in fear responses.
naming.caution: Small group, in a laboratory, without anxious participants: the study explains a possible mechanism but does not measure the effect on anxiety.

whenToPractice.title: When to Practice
items: When you notice repetitive or intrusive thoughts spinning in your mind.
Before high-pressure situations where self-doubt or worry typically arise.
During moments of overwhelm when thoughts feel chaotic and unmanageable.
As part of daily mindfulness practice to build awareness of thought patterns.

whatYoullNotice.title: What You Might Notice
items: Anxious thoughts feeling a little lighter
Usual thoughts that are easier to recognise
A growing ability to observe your thoughts without reacting straight away

observation.title: Observer Stance
observation.description: Approach your thoughts with curiosity, not judgment. You're a scientist studying your mind, not a critic condemning it.

consistency.title: Build the Habit
consistency.description: Practice labeling throughout the day, not just during anxiety spikes. Regular use strengthens your ability to create distance from thoughts.

simplicity.title: Keep Labels Simple
simplicity.description: Use short, clear labels like "worry," "judgment," or "catastrophizing." You're identifying patterns, not writing essays.
